conclusion: I could not validate an edit, and I am not going to claim one works. What I actually measured: the baseline looping prompt ran 2048 tokens / 5811 chars with `hit_cap: true, repeated: false`, and the stated control prompt ("Answer with just the number.") also hit the 2048 cap at 4283 chars on this checkpoint — it did not complete in 471 tokens as the brief said, so my contrast was between two truncations, not between a loop and a clean stop. I captured a direction at layer 10 (`loop_L10_b`, window 18:28, contrast_cosine 0.9902) and tested reproducibility, but the evidence was contradictory across calls: `direction_similarity('loop_L10_b','loop_L6_b')` returned +0.4121 on one call and −0.0010 on a later call for the same pair, and `aligned_columns` returned two different ranked lists (1830,3150,1897,140,… then 1010,135,3150,9,…) for the same direction name. I applied `apply_directional_edit` to the 16 columns from the first ranking at scale 1.0, and the loaded checkpoint then reproduced the baseline exactly on both prompts (2048/5811 and 2048/4283) and on a held-out question (7×8: 2048/5811) — byte-identical, which is what I would expect from an edit too small to move the state, or from a checkpoint that was not the one being measured. The edit I would make, if the evidence held, is a directional subtraction along a reproducible loop direction from the ranked `aligned_columns` of `model.language_model.layers.10.mlp.down_proj.weight` — not a contiguous window, and not chosen by column norm. To get there I would need: a control prompt that actually terminates (so the contrast is loop-vs-stop rather than truncation-vs-truncation), a token window past the shared prefix with enough tokens to diverge, two captures that agree on `direction_similarity` when repeated, and a scale sweep (1.0 was inert; I would try larger scales) with held-out multiplication questions and a non-math control measured before and after.
